title: OS command execution via {sink} ({lang}) — review required
description: The {lang} sink {sink} hands its argument to a command shell or process launcher. If any part of the argument derives from untrusted input, an attacker can inject extra commands. This lexical rule flags the sink; the reviewer confirms every argument is trusted or safely separated from the command.
remediation: Avoid the sink: use argument-vector APIs ({safe}) so untrusted data never passes through a shell. If a shell is unavoidable, pin an allowlist of commands and quote every interpolated value.
limitation: Lexical, line-based: any {sink} call matches, including fully trusted invocations. Dataflow from untrusted input is not proven — treat every hit as review-required.
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on the {sink} call in {lang} code.
fp: Trusted, hardcoded commands (no variables) are the common false positive; confirm no interpolated input before dismissing.
recordDesc: In {lang}, {sink} executes operating-system commands. The weakness mechanics are identical across languages — shell metacharacters in untrusted input break out of the intended command — but the concrete sink spelling, argument conventions, and safe alternative ({safe}) are {lang}-specific.
applicability: {lang} codebases that launch external processes through {sink}; single-line lexical scope.
risk: Unauthenticated command execution when untrusted input reaches the sink; HIGH severity because exploitation is typically trivial and impact is full process compromise.
why: {sink} passes its argument to command execution in {lang}, so untrusted input reaching it becomes command injection.
fix: Replace {sink} with {safe}, passing untrusted data as separate arguments, never interpolated into a command string.
If a shell is required, restrict the command to a fixed allowlist and validate every argument against it.
Re-run the scan and confirm no {sink} call remains reachable from untrusted input.
verifyT: Rescan shows no {sink} reachable from untrusted input, and command tests with metacharacter input execute safely.

c: execve-family calls with an argument vector
lua: an argument-vector launcher instead of the shell
cpp: fork plus exec with an argument vector
c:popen: fork plus exec with an argument vector
vbnet: Process.Start with an ArgumentList and no shell

title: Dynamic code evaluation via {sink} ({lang}) — review required
description: The {lang} sink {sink} parses and runs a string as code. If the string contains untrusted input, an attacker achieves code execution in the application. This lexical rule flags the sink; the reviewer confirms every evaluated string is trusted or replaced with data-only parsing.
remediation: Remove the evaluation: parse data with {safe} instead of running it as code. If evaluation is unavoidable, run it in a sandbox with no sensitive authority.
limitation: Lexical, line-based: any {sink} call matches, including trusted uses such as local tooling. Whether the evaluated string is attacker-controlled needs human review.
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on the {sink} call in {lang} code.
fp: Build scripts, REPL helpers, and test harnesses evaluating trusted strings are the common false positives.
recordDesc: In {lang}, {sink} turns a string into running code. Evaluation sinks collapse the data/code boundary, so any untrusted bytes in the string become an injection primitive. The {lang}-specific remedy is data-only handling via {safe}.
applicability: {lang} codebases that build code or expressions from strings via {sink}; single-line lexical scope.
risk: Code execution in the application process when untrusted input reaches the sink; HIGH severity because evaluation sinks rarely constrain what the injected code can do.
why: {sink} evaluates strings as {lang} code, so untrusted input reaching it becomes code injection.
fix: Replace {sink} with {safe} so untrusted input stays data, never code.
If evaluation must stay, isolate it in a sandbox without file, network, or credential access.
Re-run the scan and confirm no {sink} call remains reachable from untrusted input.
verifyT: Rescan shows no {sink} reachable from untrusted input, and injection probes stay inert data.

title: Unsafe deserialization via {sink} ({lang}) — review required
description: The {lang} sink {sink} rebuilds objects from bytes, and hostile bytes can instantiate dangerous classes or run callbacks during decoding. This lexical rule flags the sink; the reviewer confirms the input source is trusted or switches to a data-only format.
remediation: Decode untrusted input with {safe} instead of object deserialization. If object graphs are required, sign the bytes and verify before decoding.
limitation: Lexical, line-based: any {sink} call matches, including decoding of trusted local state. Trust in the byte source needs human review.
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on the {sink} call in {lang} code.
fp: Loading trusted session checkpoints or local caches is the common false positive; confirm the bytes cannot arrive from the network.
recordDesc: In {lang}, {sink} performs object deserialization: bytes select classes and set fields, so a hostile payload can drive gadget chains or execute callbacks. The {lang}-specific remedy is data-only decoding via {safe}.
applicability: {lang} codebases decoding persisted or received bytes through {sink}; single-line lexical scope.
risk: Object injection leading to code execution or state corruption when hostile bytes reach the sink; HIGH severity because payloads are compact and often unauthenticated.
why: {sink} deserializes {lang} objects from bytes, so hostile input can trigger gadget execution during decoding.
fix: Replace {sink} with {safe} for any bytes that cross a trust boundary.
If object graphs must persist, authenticate the bytes (MAC/signature) and verify before decoding.
Re-run the scan and confirm no {sink} call remains reachable from untrusted bytes.
verifyT: Rescan shows no {sink} reachable from untrusted bytes, and hostile payloads decode to inert data or fail closed.

title: MD5 use via {sink} ({lang}) — review required
description: The {lang} call {sink} computes MD5, which is broken for security purposes (collisions are practical). It is unacceptable for passwords, signatures, or integrity of untrusted data, but still fine for non-security checksums. This lexical rule cannot tell the use case — treat every hit as review-required.
remediation: Use {safe} for any security purpose. Keep MD5 only for non-security checksums with a comment saying so.
limitation: Lexical, line-based: matches any {sink} call regardless of purpose. Bare md5() calls belong to the generic rule; other weak algorithms are separate rules.
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on the {sink} call in {lang} code.
fp: Deduplication, etag, and cache-key checksums are the common false positives; they need only a justifying comment.
recordDesc: In {lang}, {sink} computes MD5. Collision attacks let an attacker forge a second input with the same digest, which defeats signatures and integrity checks while leaving non-security checksums unaffected. The {lang}-specific remedy is {safe}.
applicability: {lang} codebases hashing data through {sink}; single-line lexical scope.
risk: Forged integrity values and signatures when MD5 protects untrusted data; LOW severity as a default because checksum uses dominate, raised on review when the digest is security-relevant.
why: {sink} computes MD5 in {lang}, whose collisions defeat any security reliance on the digest.
fix: Replace {sink} with {safe} wherever the digest protects passwords, signatures, or untrusted data.
For remaining checksum uses, add a comment stating MD5 is intentional and non-security.
Re-run the scan and confirm every remaining hit carries that justification.
verifyT: Rescan shows no unjustified {sink}, and security digests verify under the replacement.

title: MD5 selected by name ({lang}) — review required
description: Security code in {lang} selects MD5 by algorithm name: {sink}. MD5 collisions are practical, so the selection is unsafe for passwords, signatures, or integrity of untrusted data. This lexical rule flags the selection; the reviewer confirms the use is a non-security checksum or upgrades it.
remediation: Select {safe} instead of MD5 for any security purpose. Keep MD5 only for non-security checksums with a comment saying so.
limitation: Lexical, line-based: matches the MD5 name regardless of purpose. Call-shaped MD5 uses are separate rules.
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on the MD5 selection in {lang} code.
fp: Checksum and fingerprint selections are the common false positives; they need only a justifying comment.
recordDesc: In {lang}, naming MD5 ({sink}) requests a broken digest. Name-selected digests hide inside factory calls, so reviewers must check the string, not just the call. The {lang}-specific remedy is selecting {safe}.
applicability: {lang} codebases selecting digests by name; single-line lexical scope.
risk: Same as any MD5 use: forged digests where security is assumed; LOW default severity, raised when the digest guards trust.
why: {lang} code selects MD5 ({sink}), whose collisions defeat security reliance on the resulting digest.
fix: Replace the MD5 selection with {safe} wherever the digest is security-relevant.
For remaining checksum uses, add a comment stating MD5 is intentional and non-security.
Re-run the scan and confirm every remaining hit carries that justification.
verifyT: Rescan shows no unjustified MD5 selection, and security digests verify under the replacement.

recordDesc: In {lang}, {sink} computes SHA-1. Public collision demonstrations ended SHA-1's suitability for signatures and integrity, though content addressing and legacy interop remain legitimate. The {lang}-specific remedy is {safe}.

For remaining compatibility uses, add a comment stating SHA-1 is intentional.
Re-run the scan and confirm every remaining hit carries that justification.

cweDef.name: Use of Insufficiently Random Values
cweDef.summary: Security decisions use a predictable generator, so an attacker can guess tokens, nonces, or temporary secrets.

title: Predictable randomness via {sink} ({lang}) — review required
description: The {lang} call {sink} draws from a non-cryptographic generator. Its output is predictable from past values or seed, so tokens, nonces, and temporary secrets built on it can be guessed. This lexical rule flags the call; the reviewer confirms the value is non-security or switches to {safe}.
remediation: Draw security values from {safe}. Keep the fast generator only for simulations, games, and sampling with a comment saying so.
limitation: Lexical, line-based: matches any {sink} call regardless of purpose; no-arg generator forms are separate rules.
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on the {sink} call in {lang} code.
fp: Simulations, shuffling, test data, and games are the common false positives.
recordDesc: In {lang}, {sink} is a statistical generator, not a cryptographic one: observing outputs reveals the state, and default seeds repeat across runs. Security values need unpredictability, which only {safe} provides in {lang}.
applicability: {lang} codebases drawing random values through {sink}; single-line lexical scope.
risk: Guessed session tokens, reset links, and nonces when predictable output guards access; MEDIUM severity, HIGH when the value directly authenticates.
why: {sink} is predictable in {lang}, so security values drawn from it can be guessed by an attacker.
fix: Replace {sink} with {safe} for tokens, nonces, salts, and secrets.
For remaining statistical uses, add a comment stating predictability is acceptable.
Re-run the scan and confirm every security draw uses the cryptographic generator.
verifyT: Rescan shows no {sink} feeding security values, and token prediction tests fail.

title: Predictable generator use ({lang}) — review required
description: Code in {lang} draws from a non-cryptographic generator: {sink}. Output is predictable, so security values built on it can be guessed. This lexical rule flags the use; the reviewer confirms the value is non-security or switches to {safe}.
limitation: Lexical, line-based: matches the generator regardless of purpose. Argument-taking generator calls are separate rules.
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on the generator use in {lang} code.
fp: Test fixtures and simulations are the common false positives.
recordDesc: In {lang}, {sink} exposes a predictable generator. Default seeds and observable state make every output guessable, which is fine for sampling but fatal for tokens. The {lang}-specific remedy is {safe}.
applicability: {lang} codebases instantiating or reading the generator; single-line lexical scope.
risk: Guessed security values; LOW default severity because these forms are often test-only, raised when the value guards access.
why: {lang} code uses a predictable generator ({sink}) whose outputs an attacker can guess.
fix: Replace the generator with {safe} for security values.
For remaining statistical uses, add a comment stating predictability is acceptable.
Re-run the scan and confirm security draws use the cryptographic source.
verifyT: Rescan shows no unjustified generator use feeding security values.
